name: Adductor longus and brevis (with gracilis, pectineus)
notes: Functional medial-compartment adductor group folded into one row (adductor magnus is split out separately because of its hip-extensor hamstring portion). ADDUCTOR LONGUS: adducts and flexes the hip (openstax: 'the adductor longus flexes the thigh'). ADDUCTOR BREVIS: deep to longus, adducts and assists hip flexion. GRACILIS: the only biarticular member - strap-like, adducts the thigh AND flexes/internally-rotates the leg at the knee, inserting at the pes anserinus (origin pubis); crosses hip and knee. PECTINEUS: in the femoral triangle, adducts and flexes the hip. All chiefly obturator nerve (pectineus also femoral). LENGTH BIAS: gracilis is the biarticular member of this group (crosses hip and knee); hip-abducted/extended positions stretch the adductors - the wide stance of a sumo/wide squat or a hip abduction at length biases the group as adductors. All can medially or laterally rotate the thigh depending on foot placement. Antagonist of the hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus, TFL).

name: Adductor magnus
notes: Largest adductor; medial-compartment muscle with two functional portions. The adductor (pubofemoral) portion adducts and assists hip flexion; the posterior 'hamstring'/ischiocondylar portion (ischial tuberosity origin, adductor-tubercle insertion) is a strong HIP EXTENSOR, so adductor magnus contributes meaningfully to hip extension alongside the glutes/hamstrings - the openstax text notes adductor magnus extends the thigh while adductor longus flexes it. Can medially or laterally rotate the thigh depending on foot placement. Dual innervation: obturator nerve (adductor part) + sciatic/tibial (hamstring part). Antagonist of the hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus, TFL).

name: Anconeus
notes: Small triangular muscle at the lateral posterior elbow (origin lateral epicondyle of humerus, insertion lateral olecranon / posterior ulna). Assists the triceps in elbow extension and stabilizes the elbow joint, abducting the ulna during pronation. Not independently trainable in practice - it is co-active with triceps in every extension movement; enumerated here for completeness as the accessory elbow extensor. Note-level per PLAN.

name: Biceps brachii (long head)
notes: Long head originates on the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, so it crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow and proximal radioulnar joint - it is the biarticular head and the one bias-able by shoulder position. Flexes and supinates the forearm and assists shoulder flexion; also resists glenohumeral dislocation. EMG paper (Oliveira et al.) shows the incline curl pre-stretches the long head by placing the shoulder in extension/hyperextension behind the torso, putting it on length; the preacher curl with the shoulder flexed pre-shortens it and only loads a short elbow-angle range. This shoulder-extended stretch is the targetable long-length position. Strongest single-joint biceps action is elbow flexion, with supination torque highest near 90 deg elbow.

name: Biceps brachii (short head)
notes: Short head originates on the coracoid process of the scapula (shared with coracobrachialis), so it too crosses the shoulder, elbow, and proximal radioulnar joints. Same actions as the long head - elbow flexion, forearm supination, shoulder flexion/adduction assist. Kept as a distinct row because the two biceps heads are conventionally trained as bias-able sub-units (e.g. narrow vs wide-grip / preacher curls shift relative demand); the long head, lying more lateral and crossing further behind the glenoid, is the one most lengthened by shoulder extension. Biceps brachii is one of the most anatomically variable muscles (3-7 supernumerary heads reported, 3-headed variant most common).

name: Brachialis
notes: The pure elbow flexor: originates on the distal anterior humerus, inserts on the coronoid process / ulnar tuberosity, so it acts only at the elbow and is unaffected by forearm rotation (inserts on ulna, not radius - no supination/pronation role). Lies deep to the biceps and provides the bulk of elbow-flexion power. Because its leverage does not change with forearm position, neutral/pronated-grip curls (hammer, reverse) shift demand onto it relative to the biceps. Monoarticular, so no length-bias position.

name: Triceps brachii (lateral head)
notes: Monoarticular elbow extensor: origin on the posterior humerus above the radial groove, insertion on the olecranon. Acts only at the elbow, so it is not affected by shoulder position - loaded across all triceps movements (pressdowns, dips, close-grip press). Most superficial/lateral of the three heads.

name: Triceps brachii (long head)
notes: The only biarticular triceps head - originates on the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, so it crosses the shoulder and extends/adducts the arm in addition to extending the elbow. It is placed on stretch (targetable long-length) when the shoulder is FLEXED / overhead, because the proximal attachment moves away from the elbow as the arm goes overhead. Overhead extensions therefore bias the long head; pressdowns with the arm at the side leave it relatively shortened. Distinct from the two monoarticular heads.

name: Triceps brachii (medial head)
notes: Monoarticular elbow extensor: origin on the posterior humerus below the radial groove, insertion on the olecranon. Deep workhorse head active across the full extension range and at all loads; unaffected by shoulder position. Together the three heads insert via the common triceps tendon on the olecranon process of the ulna.

name: Erector spinae
notes: The intrinsic (deep) extensor mass of the back running either side of the spine, conventionally enumerated as one functional column with three vertical columns/heads from lateral to medial: ILIOCOSTALIS (most lateral, ribs/angle of ribs), LONGISSIMUS (intermediate, the largest), SPINALIS (most medial, to spinous processes). Spans the full vertebral column from sacrum/iliac crest to the skull. Bilateral contraction extends the spine (deadlift/back-extension lockout, posture); unilateral contraction laterally flexes and rotates the trunk to the same side. Spans many intervertebral joints (not 'biarticular' in the limb sense). Functions isometrically as an anti-flexion trunk stabilizer under axial load; the deep transversospinalis (multifidus, semispinalis) and serratus posterior are folded in here as non-independently-trainable postural extensors. Antagonist to the abdominal flexors (anti-extension core).

name: Latissimus dorsi
notes: Broad fan-shaped axial back muscle; the prime vertical/horizontal puller (lat pulldown, pull-up, row). Origin spans T7-T12 spinous processes, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lower ribs 9-12, inserting at the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus, so it extends, adducts and internally rotates the humerus and depresses the scapula/shoulder girdle. HD-EMG shows the excitation centroid shifts laterally with a front-bar (frontal-trajectory) lat pulldown vs a more medial/scapular-adduction-driven pattern with the bar behind the neck, evidence of regionally biasable fascicles by arm path; surface-EMG grip/forearm-orientation studies, however, find LD activation stays roughly constant (~45-62% MVC) across pronated/supinated/neutral and wide/narrow grips, so grip choice barely shifts overall LD recruitment. Primary back-width target for the routine generator.

name: Levator scapulae
notes: Transverse processes of C1-C4 to the superior medial border (superior angle) of the scapula. Elevates the scapula and downwardly rotates the glenoid; with the scapula fixed it laterally flexes the cervical spine. Co-active in shrugs and the top of upright rows; a common neck/upper-back postural muscle. (StatPearls' function line copying the latissimus humeral actions is an evident text error in that source; the elevator/downward-rotator role is the standard kinesiology description.)

name: Rhomboid major
notes: Deep to trapezius; T2-T5 spinous processes to the medial (vertebral) border of the scapula below the spine. Retracts the scapula and rotates the glenoid cavity inferiorly (downward rotation), assists elevation; a postural scapular adductor co-active with middle trapezius in rows and pulldowns. Functionally near-identical to rhomboid minor (kept as a separate row only because conventionally enumerated; the two are frequently treated together as 'rhomboids').

name: Rhomboid minor
notes: Small band superior to rhomboid major; nuchal ligament and C7-T1 spinous processes to the superior medial border of the scapula. Same actions as rhomboid major - scapular retraction, downward (inferior) rotation of the glenoid, and elevation. Trained indistinguishably from rhomboid major and middle trapezius in any scapular-retraction movement.

name: Serratus anterior
notes: Sits at the scapula on the lateral rib cage (origin ribs 1-8/9, insertion anterior surface of the scapular medial border); grouped here for the scapular cross-reference though it lies on the anterolateral thorax and is conventionally cross-listed to chest/shoulder. Protracts the scapula (punch, push-up-plus, bench lockout) and, paired with upper+lower trapezius as a force couple, upwardly rotates the scapula for overhead reach. Long-thoracic-nerve (C5-C7) palsy denervates it, producing scapular winging. Antagonist to the rhomboids/middle trapezius in the protraction-retraction pair.

name: Teres major
notes: Inferior angle/posterior surface of the scapula to the medial lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus, paralleling the latissimus dorsi insertion. Extends, adducts and internally rotates the humerus - the 'lat's little helper,' co-active in every pulldown/row and pullover; not part of the rotator cuff. Internal rotator, so antagonist to the external-rotator cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor).

name: Trapezius
notes: Large diamond-shaped scapular muscle conventionally trained as three functionally distinct regions sharing accessory-nerve (CN XI) innervation, hence heads rather than separate rows. UPPER (occiput/nuchal ligament to lateral clavicle+acromion): elevates the scapula (shrug) and assists cervical extension; biased by shrugs/upright holds. MIDDLE (C7-T3 to scapular spine): retracts the scapula (rows, reverse fly) - EMG-active and centroid shifts medially with front-bar pulldowns reflecting greater scapular adduction. LOWER (T4-T12 to medial scapular spine): depresses the scapula and, together with upper+serratus anterior as a force couple, upwardly rotates it during overhead motion (key for shoulder-friendly pressing and pulldown). Mid and lower trapezius are co-targeted in horizontal pulls and the lat pulldown as scapular stabilizers.

name: Fibularis (peroneal) group
notes: The lateral-compartment muscles fibularis longus (peroneus longus) and fibularis brevis (peroneus brevis), folded into one functional-group row (note-level per the leaf granularity rule - not independently trained for hypertrophy). They are the primary everters of the foot with a secondary plantarflexion action (eversion moment arm F=3, plantarflexion S=3 for each), and are key lateral-ankle stabilizers (eccentric brake against inversion sprains). Fibularis longus crosses the sole to support the transverse arch; fibularis brevis inserts on the 5th metatarsal base. Frontal-plane antagonists of the tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior (their eversion opposes the tibialis inversion).

name: Gastrocnemius
notes: The superficial two-headed calf muscle and the leg's only biarticular muscle in this region, crossing both knee and ankle; with the soleus it forms the triceps surae, the two providing ~80% of plantarflexion force via the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon. AUTHORITY ROW on biarticular calf length_bias: because it crosses the knee, the gastroc is lengthened knee-extended and shortened knee-flexed, so its plantarflexion (and the targetable training stimulus) is maximal with the knee straight and minimal with the knee bent - standing calf-raise (knee-extended) drove 9-12% gastroc hypertrophy vs ~0-2% (non-significant) seated/knee-90deg, while the monoarticular soleus grew equally in both (gastroc-vs-soleus knee-angle principle; standing-vs-seated). Electrical-stimulation torque-angle work confirms the GA produces its greatest plantarflexion moment knee-straight + ankle-dorsiflexed (its longest length) - unusual for a biarticular muscle, whose optimum is usually not its longest length, but the knee/ankle ROM does not stretch it past optimum. As a knee flexor it is weak (small 3rd-class lever at the knee) and only contributes meaningfully when the knee is near-extended (<~15deg flexion); plantarflexion dominates via the powerful 2nd-class ankle lever. The medial/lateral heads are innervated by separate nerve branches and show region-specific activation (HD-EMG); the medial head also carries a small inversion and the lateral head a small eversion (frontal) moment arm at the ankle.

name: Plantaris
notes: Small vestigial muscle running obliquely between gastrocnemius and soleus in the superficial posterior compartment, with a long thin tendon to the calcaneus. Biarticular (crosses knee and ankle) so nominally a weak knee flexor + plantarflexor sharing the gastrocnemius's knee-extended length_bias (lengthened knee-straight), but its force contribution is trivial; absent in ~7-10% of people. Note-level / enumerate-only (no independent training relevance; cannot be biased apart from the triceps surae). Its tendon is harvested as a graft for ligament/tendon repair.

name: Popliteus
notes: Small deep muscle at the back of the knee (one of the four deep posterior-compartment muscles) acting only at the knee, not the ankle. Internally rotates the tibia on the femur (or externally rotates the femur on a fixed tibia) to 'unlock' the fully extended/screw-home knee at the start of flexion, and assists knee flexion (knee sagittal + transverse moment arms). Note-level / enumerate-only - a postural/stabilizing unlocker, not a hypertrophy target; listed for anatomical completeness of the posterior leg.

name: Soleus
notes: Wide, flat monoarticular plantarflexor lying deep to the gastrocnemius; joins it to form the triceps surae and the Achilles tendon (the two ~80% of plantarflexion force). Because it crosses ONLY the ankle, its length and force are unaffected by knee angle, so the knee-bent (seated, knee-90deg) position ISOLATES it: with the knee flexed the gastroc is slackened/shortened and contributes little plantarflexion, leaving the soleus as the prime mover - this is why seated calf-raise targets soleus and standing targets gastroc. In the standing-vs-seated MRI trial the soleus hypertrophied equally (~2-3%) in both knee positions while the gastroc only grew standing, the cleanest demonstration of the mono- vs bi-articular knee-angle dissociation. Soleus is highly fatigue-resistant (postural antigravity muscle, type-I dominant) and, like the whole triceps surae, relatively resistant to hypertrophy.

name: Tibialis posterior
notes: Deepest of the four deep posterior-compartment muscles (with popliteus, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus). The primary inverter of the foot and a secondary ankle plantarflexor, and the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch (the largest frontal/inversion moment arm among ankle muscles, F=7, plus a plantarflexion moment arm S=5). Note-level / enumerate-only for a hypertrophy program (no common direct exercise; trained incidentally by plantarflexion and arch/foot work). Direct frontal-plane antagonist of the fibularis/peroneal everters; synergist with tibialis anterior for inversion.

name: Pectoralis major
notes: Thick fan-shaped prime mover of the anterior thorax; the primary 'chest' muscle for pressing/flye work. Three fiber regions converge to insert on the lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus. Clavicular head (origin: medial clavicle) is biased by higher/incline pressing and shoulder-flexion-dominant work (it has an upper-fiber line of pull that flexes the already-extended arm); the larger sternocostal head (origin: sternum + costal cartilages ribs 1-6) and the abdominal/costal fibers (origin including external oblique aponeurosis) are biased by flat/decline pressing and pure horizontal adduction. All three heads share shoulder adduction, horizontal adduction and internal rotation; the clavicular head additionally flexes the shoulder. Heads are trained-bias variants of one muscle (incline vs flat/decline), NOT separately innervated independent muscles, so modeled as one row with a heads[] array. Innervation: medial + lateral pectoral nerves. (libretexts table mislabels its insertion/origin in places; StatPearls origin/insertion used as the authority.)

name: Pectoralis minor
notes: Deep to pectoralis major; a scapular stabilizer, NOT a humeral mover. Origin ribs 3-5 near their costal cartilages, insertion onto the coracoid process of the scapula. Acts on the pectoral girdle: depresses, protracts (with downward/inferior tilt) the scapula and assists forced inhalation as an accessory; tightness contributes to a protracted/anteriorly-tilted scapula. Antagonized by the trapezius (lower fibers oppose its depression/downward-tilt; upper fibers oppose via elevation) and balanced against the serratus anterior in scapular positioning. Not directly programmed in a hypertrophy PPL (enumerate-only); relevant to posture/scapular mechanics rather than a target of chest pressing. Innervation: medial pectoral nerve.

name: External oblique
notes: Most superficial of the three flat lateral abdominal muscles; fascicles run inferomedially ('hands sliding into front pants pockets'), originating from ribs 5-12 and inserting on the linea alba, pubis, and anterior iliac crest. Working with the contralateral internal oblique it produces trunk rotation to the OPPOSITE side (left external oblique rotates trunk right) plus lateral flexion (frontal) and assists trunk flexion (sagittal). Targeted by twisting / anti-rotation work. Monoarticular spinal muscle, no length-bias position.

name: Internal oblique
notes: Intermediate flat lateral abdominal muscle lying just deep to the external oblique; fascicles run superomedially, PERPENDICULAR to the external oblique (the 'thumbs-up' direction), from the iliac crest/inguinal ligament/thoracolumbar fascia to the lower ribs and linea alba. Produces trunk rotation to the SAME side (ipsilateral) - it pairs with the contralateral external oblique in a rotational couple - plus lateral flexion and assists trunk flexion. Monoarticular spinal muscle, no length-bias position.

name: Quadratus lumborum
notes: Forms the POSTERIOR abdominal wall (with psoas major and iliacus); runs from the iliac crest/iliolumbar ligament to rib 12 and the transverse processes of L1-L4. Acts in the frontal plane as a lateral flexor of the trunk and as a hip-hiker (elevates the ilium, e.g. side-bends, suitcase carries, offset/unilateral loading); bilaterally it depresses rib 12 and stabilizes the lumbar spine. Its functional antagonist is the contralateral quadratus lumborum (each side opposes the other in lateral flexion), so the antagonist id self-references this single muscle row. Monoarticular trunk muscle, no length-bias position.

name: Rectus abdominis
notes: The paired 'sit-up' muscle running pubic crest/symphysis to sternum (xiphoid) and costal cartilages of ribs 5-7; segmented by three tendinous intersections, producing the visible 'six-pack'. Prime mover of spinal/trunk flexion in the sagittal plane (curl-up, crunch, leg-raise via posterior pelvic tilt). Monoarticular spinal-segment muscle; no length-bias position. Antagonist to the erector spinae on the anti-extension axis.

name: Transversus abdominis
notes: Deepest of the four abdominal muscles; fascicles wrap transversely around the trunk 'like a belt' (ilium/inguinal ligament/lower-rib cartilages/thoracolumbar fascia to the linea alba). Its job is COMPRESSION of the abdominal contents and generation of intra-abdominal pressure (forced exhalation, defecation, urination, childbirth, Valsalva/bracing) rather than producing spinal movement - so it is a stabilizer with no significant agonist/antagonist movement pairing. No length-bias position (monoarticular, isometric stabilizer).

name: Brachioradialis
notes: Forearm-compartment elbow flexor (origin lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus, insertion styloid process of radius). Anatomically a posterior/radial muscle but functions as a flexor of the elbow, strongest with the forearm in a neutral (mid-prone) grip - hence its dominance in hammer and reverse curls. It also returns the forearm toward neutral from either extreme (assists pronation from a supinated start and supination from a pronated start). Crosses elbow + proximal radioulnar but both are at the same segment level, so treated as functionally monoarticular with no shoulder-dependent length-bias.

name: Finger flexors (crush-grip group)
notes: CRUSH-GRIP GROUP - keys the LEFT-PINKY constraint. The extrinsic finger flexors: flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS, intermediate layer, common flexor origin on medial epicondyle + coronoid + radius; flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of fingers 2-5 and weakly the MCPs) and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP, deep layer, origin anteromedial ulna + interosseous membrane; flexes the distal interphalangeal joints of fingers 2-5 and also flexes the wrist). Together they close the hand into a fist and generate crushing grip force; FDP is the only flexor of the DIP joints. These multi-joint tendons cross the wrist plus every finger joint, so they are placed on stretch when the wrist is extended and the fingers open (active-/passive-insufficiency interaction: making a tight fist with the wrist flexed shortens them and weakens grip; cocking the wrist into extension lengthens them and strengthens grip - the tenodesis effect). Because grip on hanging/holding exercises (deadlifts, rows, dead-hangs, loaded carries) is limited by this group and routes load through the fingers, any per-finger limitation (e.g. a left-pinky issue, finger 5 served by the medial/ulnar-nerve portion of FDP) propagates here - this is the muscle endpoint the constraints left-pinky logic keys off via the crush-grip / weight-hanging grip-pattern tags. Antagonized by extensor digitorum.

name: Pronator teres
notes: Primary forearm pronator (the deep pronator quadratus is its synergist). Two heads of origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus and the coronoid process of the ulna; inserts on the lateral mid-shaft of the radius. Turns the palm down (pronation) and weakly assists elbow flexion. Trained directly by resisted pronation (e.g. pronation/supination with a weighted bar). Antagonized by the supinator (and biceps brachii in supination). Note-level per PLAN but given its own row as the named prime pronator; pronator quadratus folded in as its synergist.

name: Supinator
notes: Deep posterior-compartment muscle that turns the palm up (supination); origin lateral epicondyle of humerus + supinator crest of ulna, wraps to insert on the proximal radius. It is the supinator that acts independently of elbow angle, whereas the biceps brachii is the powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed (~90 deg) - so neutral-elbow or extended-elbow supination isolates the supinator from the biceps. Trained by resisted supination. Antagonized by pronator teres / pronator quadratus. Note-level per PLAN, given its own row as the named prime supinator.

name: Wrist extensors (forearm extensor group)
notes: Functional group of the superficial posterior (extensor) forearm compartment, mostly arising from the common extensor origin / lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus. Members: extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis (extend + radially deviate/abduct the wrist), extensor carpi ulnaris (extends + ulnarly deviates/adducts the wrist), and extensor digitorum (extends the wrist and the fingers 2-5 at the MCP/IP joints via the extensor expansions). Trained directly by reverse/extension wrist curls and indirectly by every gripping task (they stabilize the wrist against the finger flexors). Overuse of the common extensor origin causes lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). Antagonizes the wrist flexors; extensor digitorum antagonizes the finger flexors.

name: Wrist flexors (forearm flexor group)
notes: Functional group of the superficial anterior (flexor) forearm compartment, all arising from the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Members: flexor carpi radialis (flexes + radially deviates/abducts the wrist, inserts base of metacarpals 2-3), flexor carpi ulnaris (flexes + ulnarly deviates/adducts the wrist, inserts pisiform/hamate/5th metacarpal), and palmaris longus (weak wrist flexor, tenses palmar aponeurosis; absent in ~10-15% of people, polymorphic). Trained directly by wrist curls; the radial/ulnar pair also balances wrist deviation. Overuse of the common flexor origin causes medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Antagonized by the wrist-extensor group.

name: Gluteus maximus
notes: Largest and most superficial gluteal muscle; the body's prime hip extensor and a powerful external rotator, with the upper fibers assisting hip abduction. Origin from the posterior ilium/sacrum/coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament; inserts to the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of the femur. Inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2). EMG (hamstring-glute regional study): driven hardest by hip-extension/hip-hinge moves (hip extension, cable kickbacks, RDL, step-up) and least by pure knee-flexion moves (leg curl elicits the lowest GMax of six exercises) - i.e. it is a hip-extension, not knee-flexion, muscle. Functionally antagonistic to the hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris).

name: Gluteus medius
notes: Deep to gluteus maximus; primary hip abductor and a key frontal-plane pelvic stabilizer in single-leg stance (prevents contralateral pelvic drop). Anterior fibers internally rotate and flex the hip, posterior fibers externally rotate and extend it. Origin on the lateral ilium, inserts on the greater trochanter. Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). Synergist with TFL and iliopsoas in abduction/flexion. Antagonized by the hip adductor group.

name: Gluteus minimus
notes: Smallest and deepest of the three gluteals, deep to gluteus medius. Hip abductor and internal rotator; works with gluteus medius for frontal-plane pelvic stabilization. Origin on the lateral ilium, inserts on the anterior greater trochanter. Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). Not independently trainable from gluteus medius in practice but enumerated separately. Antagonized by the hip adductor group.

name: Biceps femoris
notes: Lateral hamstring with two heads of different architecture: the LONG head crosses hip and knee (biarticular, ischial tuberosity origin, hip extension + knee flexion + tibial external rotation when knee bent; sciatic/tibial division) and is one of the most injury-prone thigh muscles; the SHORT head is MONOARTICULAR (femoral linea aspera origin, knee flexion only; sciatic/common-fibular division). Both insert on the fibular head. Single anatomical muscle so kept as one row with the long/short heads. LENGTH BIAS: hip-flexed with knee extended (e.g. RDL/stiff-leg hip hinge) places the biarticular long head on maximal stretch as a hip extensor; the short head is monoarticular and is biased by knee flexion regardless of hip angle. Regional/exercise EMG (hamstring-glute regional-emg study) shows biceps-femoris activation is exercise-dependent along its length: knee-flexion-dominant moves (Nordic curls, leg curls, cable kickbacks) drive proximal, medial and distal BF more than hip-hinge moves (RDL, step-up), with the Nordic exercise eliciting the highest BF activation overall; hip-extension/hip-hinge moves preferentially recruit BF long head and semimembranosus while knee-flexion moves favor semitendinosus and BF short head.

name: Semimembranosus
notes: Deepest medial hamstring (broad membranous proximal tendon, origin ischial tuberosity, inserts on the posteromedial tibial condyle). Biarticular: extends hip, flexes knee, internally rotates the flexed knee. Sciatic (tibial division). LENGTH BIAS: hip-flexed with knee extended places it on stretch as a hip extensor; hip-extension/hip-hinge exercises preferentially bias it (with BF long head). EMG literature shows hip-extension-dominant/hip-hinge movements preferentially recruit semimembranosus and BF long head versus knee-flexion-dominant movements that favor semitendinosus and BF short head.

name: Semitendinosus
notes: Medial hamstring; long fusiform belly ending in a long cord-like tendon (origin ischial tuberosity, inserts on the medial tibia at the pes anserinus with sartorius and gracilis). Biarticular: extends hip, flexes knee, and internally rotates the flexed knee. Sciatic (tibial division). Forms the popliteal fossa border with semimembranosus and biceps femoris. LENGTH BIAS: hip-flexed with knee extended places it on stretch as a hip extensor; knee-flexion-dominant exercises preferentially bias it relative to the rest of the hamstring group. EMG literature indicates knee-flexion-dominant exercises preferentially recruit semitendinosus (and BF short head) over the hip-extension-biased BF long head / semimembranosus.

name: Iliopsoas
notes: Primary hip flexor, a composite of PSOAS MAJOR (origin from the lumbar vertebrae T12-L5 bodies/transverse processes; also contributes to lumbar posture/anterior pelvic tilt) and ILIACUS (origin from the iliac fossa); they merge and insert via a common tendon on the lesser trochanter of the femur. Lumbar plexus / femoral nerve (psoas L1-L3, iliacus L2-L4). Synergist with rectus femoris and sartorius in hip flexion. The dominant antagonist of the gluteus maximus and hamstrings in the sagittal plane (hip flexion vs hip extension). Psoas major is sometimes counted as crossing the lumbar spine, but functionally treated here as a hip-flexor crossing the hip.

name: Sartorius
notes: Longest muscle in the body; band-like, runs diagonally from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial proximal tibia (pes anserinus, with gracilis and semitendinosus). Biarticular and multiplanar: at the hip it flexes, abducts, and externally rotates; at the knee it flexes and internally rotates - the combined 'tailor's'/cross-legged-sitting action. Femoral nerve (L2-L3). Crosses both hip and knee. LENGTH BIAS: hip-extended with knee extended places this long diagonal muscle on stretch; it is biased by the combined 'cross-legged' action (hip flexion + abduction + external rotation with knee flexion).

name: Tensor fasciae latae
notes: Thick squarish muscle of the superior lateral thigh; flexes, abducts, and internally rotates the hip and tenses the iliotibial tract/band, stabilizing the lateral knee (so it crosses the knee functionally via the IT tract, hence biarticular). Acts as a synergist of gluteus medius and iliopsoas in flexing and abducting the thigh. Origin on the anterior iliac crest/ASIS region, inserts into the iliotibial tract. Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). LENGTH BIAS: hip-extended/adducted lengthens it via its IT-band attachment; it is biased in flexed/abducted/internally-rotated hip positions and assists lateral knee stability through the iliotibial tract. Note-level per the leaf plan but enumerated as its own row; antagonized by the adductors (frontal plane) and, in IT-tract tension, opposed by gluteus maximus's posterior pull.

name: Rectus femoris
notes: Only biarticular quadriceps head: superficial, nearly vertical, crossing hip and knee. Direct head from anterior inferior iliac spine, indirect head from superior acetabular ridge; inserts via quadriceps tendon to patella, then patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity. Flexes hip (with iliopsoas/sartorius) and extends knee (with vasti). LENGTH BIAS: hip-extended (with knee flexed) puts it on stretch; it is most targetable as a knee extensor when the hip is extended/neutral rather than flexed. Active insufficiency: with the hip already flexed (seated), the full knee extension it can produce weakens because it is simultaneously shortened at both joints, so it is a weak knee extender in the sitting/hip-flexed position; passive insufficiency at full knee flexion limits hip extension. EMG (Miyamoto 2012) shows RF is differentially controlled along its length: during hip-flexion MVC the distal region activates significantly less than middle/proximal, and overall RF activation in hip flexion is lower than in knee extension - the distal region cannot be fully driven during hip flexion. Most frequently strained quadriceps muscle (the 'kicking muscle').

name: Vastus intermedius
notes: Lies between vastus lateralis and vastus medialis and deep to rectus femoris. Deepest, least visible quadriceps head; monoarticular knee extensor sharing the common quadriceps/patellar tendon. Femoral nerve (L2-L4). The articularis genus (small slip tensing the knee-joint capsule) is associated with it.

name: Vastus lateralis
notes: Largest of the three vasti, on the lateral aspect of the thigh. Monoarticular knee extensor; part of the quadriceps femoris group, sharing the common quadriceps/patellar tendon. Femoral nerve (L2-L4). Not subject to active/passive insufficiency, so trainable through full knee ROM at any hip angle.

name: Vastus medialis
notes: On the medial aspect of the thigh; its oblique distal fibers (vastus medialis obliquus) help track the patella medially, prominent near terminal knee extension. Monoarticular knee extensor, part of quadriceps femoris, shares quadriceps/patellar tendon. Femoral nerve (L2-L4).

name: Tibialis anterior
notes: Long thick muscle on the lateral surface of the tibia in the anterior compartment; the principal dorsiflexor of the ankle and the chief shin muscle, with a secondary inversion action (largest dorsiflexion moment arm of any ankle muscle, S=16, plus a frontal/inversion moment arm, F=8). It is the direct antagonist of the triceps surae (plantarflexion) - in the two-joint-link model the tibialis-anterior and gastrocnemius are the opposed mono-/bi-articular force pair at the ankle whose combined output the model resolves. Antagonist to the fibularis/peroneal group in the frontal plane (its inversion opposes their eversion) but synergist with tibialis posterior for inversion.

name: Coracobrachialis
notes: Small anterior-arm muscle crossing only the glenohumeral joint (origin: coracoid process of the scapula, shared with the biceps short head; insertion: medial aspect of the mid-humeral shaft). Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder and acts as a weak humeral-head stabilizer; it does NOT cross the elbow, so it is monoarticular despite sitting in the anterior arm compartment. Not directly programmed (note-level / enumerate-only); recruited as a synergist in shoulder flexion and adduction. Innervation: musculocutaneous nerve (C5,C6,C7).

name: Anterior deltoid (deltoid, anterior/clavicular part)
notes: Anterior (clavicular) head of the three-headed deltoid; modeled as its own row because the deltoid is the canonical case where heads are trained as functionally distinct muscles (front raise / overhead-press front-bias vs lateral raise vs reverse fly). Origin lateral third of the clavicle, insertion deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. Prime mover of shoulder flexion; also internally rotates and horizontally adducts the arm, and assists abduction. Heavily co-recruited in horizontal and vertical pressing, so it gets indirect volume from chest/shoulder press work. Innervation: axillary nerve (C5,C6). Direct antagonist of the posterior deltoid.

name: Lateral deltoid (deltoid, middle/acromial part)
notes: Middle/acromial head of the deltoid (origin: acromion), insertion deltoid tuberosity. The primary abductor of the arm through the mid-range of frontal-plane elevation (supraspinatus initiates the first ~15-30 deg, then the lateral deltoid takes over). Multipennate architecture makes it the strongest abductor head; targeted by lateral raises and upright-row-style abduction. The frontal-plane width muscle of the shoulder. Innervation: axillary nerve.

name: Posterior deltoid (deltoid, posterior/spinal part)
notes: Posterior head of the deltoid (origin scapular spine, insertion deltoid tuberosity); the three deltoid heads are conventionally trained as distinct muscles, hence a separate row from anterior/lateral deltoid. Horizontally abducts (reverse fly, face pull), extends and externally rotates the humerus - the prime mover of horizontal pulling at the shoulder and a synergist in rows/pulldowns. EMG rises markedly with a wide-pronated grip at 30 degrees trunk inclination in the lat pulldown, and is most excited (more elongated) when the arm acts in front of the body. Direct antagonist of the anterior deltoid and a counter to the pressing-dominant pec/front-delt in push-pull balance. Innervation: axillary nerve.

name: Infraspinatus
notes: Rotator-cuff muscle in the infraspinous fossa (below the scapular spine) inserting on the middle facet of the greater tubercle; the principal external (lateral) rotator of the humerus and a posterior glenohumeral stabilizer that resists posterior humeral-head translation. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve. Forms a clean antagonist pair with subscapularis (external vs internal rotation). EMG-active as a posterior-shoulder stabilizer in the lat pulldown, rising with wider/neutral grips and trunk inclination; directly targeted by external-rotation and face-pull / cuff prehab movements. Enumerate-only direct work in a hypertrophy PPL.

name: Subscapularis
notes: Largest rotator-cuff muscle and the only one on the anterior (costal) surface of the scapula (subscapular fossa) inserting on the lesser tubercle. Internally rotates and adducts the humerus and is the principal anterior glenohumeral stabilizer, resisting anterior humeral-head translation. Innervated by the upper + lower subscapular nerves. Listed under the posterior-upper / scapulohumeral cuff for completeness though its belly faces anteriorly; antagonist to the external rotators (infraspinatus, teres minor). Enumerate-only / prehab in a hypertrophy PPL.

name: Supraspinatus
notes: Rotator-cuff muscle in the supraspinous fossa (above the scapular spine) inserting on the superior facet of the greater tubercle; initiates the first ~15-30 degrees of humeral abduction before the lateral deltoid takes over, and compresses/centers the humeral head in the glenoid as a dynamic stabilizer. Suprascapular-nerve innervated. Its tendon is the most commonly impinged/torn in rotator-cuff disease (poor blood supply), so it is the headline of cuff pathology. Sits posteriorly on the scapula but acts on the same frontal-plane abduction axis as the lateral deltoid. Enumerate-only / prehab stabilizer for a hypertrophy routine; antagonist (as an abductor/elevator) to the adductors lat/pec/teres major.

name: Teres minor
notes: Rotator-cuff muscle (lateral border of the scapula to the inferior facet of the greater tubercle); externally rotates and adducts the humerus and stabilizes the glenohumeral joint by holding the humeral head against the glenoid. Innervated by the axillary nerve (unlike the suprascapular-nerve infraspinatus it works with). Trained directly by external-rotation/face-pull work; co-active as a stabilizer in rows and pulldowns. Antagonist to the internal rotators (subscapularis, teres major, lat).
